newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage-backeds mixed amid varied prepay outlooks.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage-backeds mixed amid varied prepay outlooks.

text.p: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) were narrowly mixed late Friday, recouping most losses in tandem with Treasuries, in a market divided over prepayment trends.
Prices of MBS were mixed in a range from down 1/32 to up 9/32, while 10-year Treasury notes were 4/32 higher on the day after rallying nearly one point from the day's lows.

In an erratic bond market, some analysts contended that mortgage rates had bottomed out and prepayment risks would subside, while others said rates could easily slide back down and reignite early MBS repayments.
The bond market drew support from a swift erosion in equities that triggered some safe-haven buying in short-term Treasuries. The Dow Jones Industrial Average incurred a 247.37-point slump Friday.

"The mortgage market is doing great," said one trader. "Prepayment worries have subsided, although prepayment risks haven't really changed," he said. Market participants were "probably underestimating the risks," he contended.

Among 30-year 7 1/2-percent MBS, Government National Mortgage Association bonds rose 2/32 to 101-12/32 to yield 7.32 percent, Freddie Macs gained 2/32 to 101-19/32 for a yield of 7.25 percent and Fannie Maes advanced 3/32 to 101-18/32 to yield 7.22 percent.

The MBS market performed "especially well here in the last few weeks, and when it's doing well people have greed in their eyes," the trader asserted. "When (MBS) are doing poorly, everyone is massively afraid."
Considering the lingering uncertainty about rate trends, "people probably shouldn't be overweighted in callable mortgages and I think a lot of people are."

Market participants did not expect next Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee policy meeting to sway bond prices much. Economists polled by Reuters generally believed the Federal Reserve will not alter interest rates before November.
There would be little direction to be gleened from a sparse economic calendar next week.

July housing starts were scheduled for release Tuesday, and were seen rising to an annualized rate of 1.46 million units from 1.452 million in June. Economists attributed that expected growth to lower mortgage rates, greater consumer confidence and improved weather last month.
